**Yes. He'd tell you to admit your weaknesses, and to do it on purpose.** He calls "damaging admissions" possibly his favourite copywriting tactic and says there's "nothing more powerful" [1]. His reasoning: every product has flaws, and your prospect is already thinking about them. If you say them first, you lose a little of your promise but gain trust, and in his view "trust trumps promise" [2][3]. You stand out because "what people won't say is the truth" [7].

**How to word it: "true flaw **but** the claim you want believed."** People take in whatever follows "but" [4]. Order matters. "These markers smell like crap, but they write four times longer" makes the long life believable. Flip it to "they write four times longer, but they smell like crap" and you've stressed the smell instead [5]. His other examples follow the same pattern: "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert", "our systems are incredibly boring but they work" [5]. His fullest example is a gym ad: "our gym has honestly pretty terrible parking, our AC is kind of on and off, I don't have the best equipment, but our sessions are more fun than everyone else's, 'cuz it's all we've got" [6]. He says a reader thinks "I kind of believe this guy." If the ad only said "most fun sessions," nobody would believe it, because anyone can say that [7]. Humour earns "bonus points" [6].

**His process:**
1. Write down every flaw, every customer complaint, and everything you know you could do better [6].
2. Turn each one into "flaw, but strength". The strength should be your main selling point, ideally the thing the flaw pays for. The gym can't compete on equipment, so it wins on fun.
3. Put them early, before the benefits. On sales calls he has reps open with "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad," and then list who the offer won't work for [8].
4. This lets people qualify themselves. Some will say "I could live with that," and then they believe the good part. He says buyers "want it. They just don't believe it." [9]

**When this wouldn't apply (my inference):** if your weakness is that the core promise doesn't deliver, you can't fix that with wording. His rule is that if too few people say yes, you fix the offer. Admissions only help when the flaw is real but secondary, like the parking or the ugly website. One caveat from me: the research he mentions on people believing someone who admits bias is uncited, and the rest is his own experience rather than measured data.

**Hormozi's answer:** for a paid online community, about 20% monthly churn (80% of members staying each month) is average, and the best communities stay under 10%. Make retention your top priority once churn goes above 30%, meaning fewer than 7 in 10 members stay each month. At that point he says retention is "the highest ROI lever" you have [1].

**When to worry.** He'd tell you to look at where in the customer lifecycle people leave before you look at your average. His "biggest rule" is that churn drops sharply with time. It's highest in months one to three. Once someone stays past day 90 it falls to around 10% or less, and by month six it's about 2% [2]. So if most of your cancels happen in month one, don't panic and "don't overhaul your entire business" [3]. Build a specific plan for getting people through the first month instead. Change the question from "how do I lower this number?" to "how do I get people past day 90 and past month six?" By day 90 a member needs a real outcome or change in behaviour, and by month six they need connections with other members [4]. If your community is less than three to six months old, your churn will look worse than it is, because nobody has reached the low-churn months yet.

**Why it matters even if you're average.** Going from 20% to 10% churn isn't a 10% improvement. It doubles how long the average member stays, and so doubles their lifetime value [5]. Each month, track joins against cancels and call the business growing, flat or declining based on those two numbers [6].

**What he'd have you do first:**
- Message everyone who cancels and tag their reason. Every 20 or so cancels, fix the top one or two reasons.
- Ask your longest-staying members why they stay, and do more of that.
- Cut overwhelm, which he ranks as the biggest churn driver after price [7]. Give new members a quick win within 24 hours.
- Add a discounted annual plan. Annual members decide once instead of 12 times, so they churn less [8].
- Show up in the community every day.

**What would change the answer:** his benchmarks are Skool platform averages. He says they fit online and consumer services, not things like insurance or alarm-system subscriptions. If your community is mostly annual members or charges a very high price, these numbers don't transfer directly.

It'll be the highest ROI lever." (Hormozi, *How to Get Your Customers to Stay FOREVER*, 2026-03-24, [1:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s))

Hormozi would tell you to pay off the $60k on a fixed schedule over the next few months, and to keep funding growth while you do it, but only growth you can already show pays back. He doesn't treat it as one or the other. He had almost exactly your case in 2026: Corey, who co-owns an HVAC-duct cleaning business doing about $1.25M a year, was putting about 10% of profit toward $60k of debt and planned to clear it in four to five months. Hormozi said "Okay, good" and made "continue to pay off the debt" item #2 of Corey's six priorities [1][4].

He's open that his reasons are partly emotional. He calls himself "very close to the Ramsey side" on debt [1]. His one argument is that debt adds risk, and over a long enough time that risk comes due, because businesses have slow seasons and swings [2]. He points to companies like Chick-fil-A that last for decades without debt [3]. He also says the payoff won't do much for your numbers: paying it off might add about 5% to profit, "but at least 100% in headache" [5]. The relief of not having it in the back of your mind is a big part of the point [1].

He'd also push you to look closely at what you mean by "growth." In the same consult he told Corey to keep raising ad spend every month as long as the return on ad spend and the cost per customer held. Corey was getting about 13 dollars back for every 1 spent, so Hormozi thought spend could go from $5k to as much as $30k a month [6]. If you're not sure where your customers come from, he says you have a data problem, and you fix tracking before you spend more [7]. He funded both goals with pricing, not spare cash. Corey closed more than 80% of quotes, which tells Hormozi the price is too low, so priority #1 was a 10% price increase. That worked out to about 25% more net profit, more than $100k a year [8]. So before you choose, raise prices, pay off the debt from that new margin, and send cash only to channels that have already paid you back. Avoid big bets ("no Hail Mary's") [9].

**What would change his answer:** If the "growth" you're saving for is an untested new channel, a hire or an expansion, his own rules point to paying off the debt first. If you have a channel that reliably returns several dollars per dollar and debt payments would starve it, he'd say keep funding the channel. He never ranked these two against each other directly, so that last part is my inference from his rules, not something he said.

My own view: if your debt has a low interest rate and your ads return 5–13x, holding cash for ads is the better financial choice. Hormozi's preference to pay it off is about lower risk and peace of mind, not about getting the highest return.

Hormozi would tell you to raise your prices. He has already answered this question, almost word for word. In a May 2026 consult he worked with Corey, the owner of ProShine, an HVAC duct-cleaning company doing $1.25M a year at a 38% net margin and an 82% close rate. That's your business on paper. His first recommendation was a 10% price increase.

His rule is that a close rate of 80% or more means the price is too low [1]. For a normal service like duct cleaning, he says a higher price can actually lift the close rate, because it makes the homeowner more confident you'll do the job properly [4]. A cheap quote can look like a "duct tape operation." He says owners are often "so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" [5], and that for businesses under roughly $3–5M, charging more is one of the biggest levers available [6]. Corey had already raised prices 23% on his team's earlier advice, and his close rate and revenue both went up [7].

He sets the limit with a break-even close rate: a 10% raise still makes more money as long as more than 65% of inspections close [2]. At your margin he figures a 10% raise adds about 25% to net profit, which is over $100K a year at current volume [3]. The 65% comes from the margin math. Your profit per job goes from 38% to about 48% of the old price, and 82% × 38/48 ≈ 65%. That arithmetic is my own reconstruction, but it matches his number. He called the 10% "more asking than telling" [8]. So raise prices, watch the close rate, and keep the increase as long as it stays above 65%. Fear of losing the close rate isn't a reason to hold back. With 38% margins he also said "The last thing I want to do is like break something" [9], so this is a measured step, not a huge jump.

What would change his answer: a close rate falling toward 65% after the raise, or a business that can't take more jobs. He checks supply before pushing growth, and Corey had just hired two people and bought a third van. A year after the consult, Corey reported he was on track for $2.3–2.5M.

That story isn't Hormozi's. Steven Bartlett tells it, the host of *The Diary of a CEO*, in the April 2023 episode Hormozi was on. Hormozi only reacts to it.

**Bartlett's story.** Bartlett's first company had gone public on a European exchange. While it was weighing a listing in another country, he went on a road show with 20 investment banks. They told him the same business would be worth four times more on the NASDAQ, so his net worth would be four times higher just from listing somewhere else [1]. Years later he applied that idea to his own skills: social media, marketing and storytelling. He reasoned they were worth the most to companies about to IPO, where a good story can move the valuation by hundreds of millions [2]. So he took an equity deal with a company heading to its IPO. After 9 to 12 months of what he calls "basically freelance" work, his equity was worth about $7–8M on IPO day [3]. That's why he started Flight Story, which began by working in the IPO market [4].

**Hormozi's reaction.** He agreed and folded it into two of his own ideas:
- **Sell to customers who value it most.** He gave the conversion-rate example. Lifting a $1M store by 20% earns you about $20K at a 10% cut. The same work for a $100M business earns $2M, which is "100x same work" [5]. His summary was to fish "where the whales are" [6].
- **Leverage.** Capital goes from friends and family to institutional money to public money. He brought Bartlett's story back here, calling the NASDAQ "Forex" (four-x) over the Düsseldorf exchange. There is far more capital in that market, so it's "same work more zeros" [7].

The captions have no speaker labels. I attributed the story to Bartlett because the speaker's company went public in Europe and later founded Flight Story, which is Bartlett's company. Hormozi's businesses were never publicly listed. The vault's wiki also files only Hormozi's response under his name.

Hormozi actually told him the opposite. In the roofing consult (Kaleb, Keys Roofing in St. Louis, a two-month-old company doing about $20K a month from door-knocking and referrals), he told Kaleb to put everything into door-knocking, not to move his budget into Google Ads. In that consult Google comes up only when Kaleb mentions asking customers for Google reviews.

His reasoning was that Kaleb could already close about one sale for every 20 doors he knocked. Hormozi treats that as rare: most entrepreneurs can't just go out and reliably "go get money," and he says being able to do that buys you extra lives [1][2]. A young company has little time or money, so he wanted "all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now" [1]. That meant the channel Kaleb was already good at, not a new one he'd have to learn. In his words: "you should go all in door to door… It's what you're good at… I don't think we need to be cute about this" [3][4].

To grow it, he told Kaleb to build a team of door-to-door reps (he called it a "D2D army") and to pay commission per door knocked. His example was about $10 a door: a 10% commission on a hoped-for $4K repair ticket, assuming a hired rep needs about 50 doors per sale. That way a rep can see exactly how many doors it takes to earn what they want [5]. When he recapped the plan, the first item was "go all in on door to door as primary growth engine" [6]. At the 90-day follow-up, Kaleb said revenue had gone from a little under $32K to about $247K. Those are Kaleb's figures, and the video doesn't say whether they're monthly or cumulative.

You may be thinking of a different consult ("Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger"). That business was already getting leads from Google and Facebook ads, and there his advice was to fix the landing page and improve the ads it already had, not to drop door-knocking.

What would change his answer: Kaleb's door-knocking not producing sales reliably, or Hormozi finding that something other than outbound volume was holding the business back.
